query: The complainant parked his motorcycle outside his house at night. In the morning it was gone. CCTV shows the accused pushing it away down the lane and riding off. The accused had no permission to take it and did not return it.
While the family was away at a wedding the accused entered their home through an unlatched window and removed gold ornaments and cash from an almirah in the bedroom.

The accused worked as a salesman at the complainant's cloth shop. Over four months he removed bolts of cloth from the stock room and sold them to a third party. The stock was never entrusted to him; he simply had access to the premises.

The accused was the accountant of a firm and was given charge of client deposits held in the firm's account. He transferred those deposits into an account in his wife's name and used them to buy property.
During a dispute over a boundary wall the accused struck the complainant on the forearm with an iron rod. The medical report records a fracture of the radius and fifteen days of hospitalisation.

The accused raised a stick above his head and advanced towards the complainant shouting that he would break his legs. Bystanders intervened before any blow landed. The complainant was not touched and suffered no injury.

The accused advertised a flat for sale, showed the complainant forged ownership papers, and accepted eleven lakh rupees as advance. He neither owned the flat nor had any agreement to sell it, and never intended to convey it.

Four men arrived together at the shop, having agreed beforehand to teach the shopkeeper a lesson. Two held him down while a third beat him; the fourth kept watch at the door. Only one of them actually inflicted the injuries.

The complainant parked his motorcycle outside his house at night. In the morning it was gone. CCTV shows the accused pushing it away down the lane and riding off. The accused had no permission to take it and did not return it.
The complainant was walking along the roadside using her phone when two men on a scooter slowed beside her, grabbed the phone out of her hand and accelerated away.
The accused broke the seal on a goods container on a stationary freight lorry at a transport depot and removed thirty cartons of electronics before the driver returned.

Following an argument outside a tea stall the accused drew a knife and stabbed the complainant twice in the abdomen. The complainant underwent emergency surgery and remained in intensive care for six days.

The accused ran a scheme promising forty per cent returns in ninety days, collected deposits from twenty-three people, paid the earliest few out of the later deposits, and stopped paying once collections slowed.

The accused telephoned the complainant claiming to be a bank fraud-prevention officer, gave a false employee number, and persuaded her to read out a one-time password, after which two lakh rupees left her account.

The three accused went to the victim's house together under a plan settled that morning. One waited in the car, one forced the gate, and the third assaulted the victim inside. The prosecution seeks to hold all three liable for the injuries caused by one of them.

The accused attended a family function at the complainant's house as a guest. After he left, a gold chain was found missing from the dressing table in the bedroom. Two days later he pledged the same chain at a pawn shop.

The accused told the complainant he could get her son a government job through his contacts, took three lakh rupees from her for processing fees, handed over an appointment letter that turned out to be fake, and then stopped answering her calls.
In a quarrel over a parking space the accused slapped the complainant and punched him in the face. The doctor recorded a swollen lip and bruises on the cheek and described the injuries as simple.

The accused, a truck operator, was engaged to carry two hundred bags of cement from the factory to the buyer's warehouse. He delivered only one hundred and twenty bags and sold the remaining eighty to a hardware shop on the way.

Two brothers came to the complainant's house carrying sticks after telling the neighbours they would settle scores with him. One stood in the doorway to stop him escaping while the other struck him repeatedly, fracturing his forearm.
The accused worked as a domestic help in the complainant's flat. Over several weeks she took cash and a mobile phone from her employer's cupboard; the phone was traced to her through its IMEI number.
A man on foot ran up behind the complainant while she waited at a bus stop, pulled the gold chain from her neck in one quick movement and ran off into a side lane.

The accused sold the complainant a used car for four lakh rupees, concealing that it was hypothecated to a bank and showing him a no-objection certificate that the bank had never issued. The bank later repossessed the car.
During a dispute over farmland the accused hit the complainant on the head with a brick. The complainant suffered a skull fracture and remained in hospital for twenty-five days.

The accused was the cashier of a private company and was handed the day's cash collections to deposit in the company's bank account. Instead of depositing the money he used it to repay his personal loans.
